Matt said Fellow had previously been introduced to Arrive’s data team, including Tyler and Alex, and that adoption by other teams helped prompt this broader discussion.

The Arrive participants were Eric Cameron, VP of People Operations; Nick Sarkesian, Director of Business Applications; Trina Berks, Technical Program Manager on the Business Applications team; and Lucas Cooper, Business Applications Manager who works primarily on finance applications for logistics. Nick Sarkesian said Arrive uses Okta internally and Workday as its HRIS, and that Okta connectivity would make the IT team’s work easier. Matt Brown described Fellow Pro as a plan built for teams and Enterprise as a plan built for company-wide deployments. He said Enterprise offers more robust security and Okta integrations, organization-wide administration, meeting analytics, and the ability to standardize and track one-on-ones across the organization. Analytics can help identify which managers are using Fellow and meeting agendas, and which might need additional support.

Matt Brown said Fellow Enterprise includes OKR tracking and feedback functionality, positioning Fellow as a centralized source of truth rather than having information spread across multiple providers. In response to Nick Sarkesian’s question about how OKRs are populated and managed, Matt said analytics can be set up for the entire organization or a single team, and Fellow would work with Arrive’s senior leadership team to import objectives. The explanation concerned a MATLAB chirpTone function that takes duration T, starting frequency f1, ending frequency f2, and sampling rate fs, and generates a sine-wave chirp. Its example call was chirpTone(10,1000,2000,4000), with soundsc suggested for playback.

On 2023-05-01, the user said they liked a formal, human-sounding explanation of digital signal processing and MATLAB code, and asked that the explanation justify why the frequency-vector expression works rather than merely state the formula.

The user was working on a formal explanation of a MATLAB function named chirpTone, which takes duration T in seconds, initial frequency f1 in Hz, final frequency f2 in Hz, and sampling rate fs in samples per second, and returns a column vector for a chirp tone. The example call was chirpTone(10,1000,2000,4000), producing a 10-second tone sweeping from 1000 Hz to 2000 Hz at 4000 samples per second.

The explanation the user requested describes the frequency vector as a linear interpolation from f1 to f2: divide the total frequency change (f2−f1) by the number of intervals (length(t)−1), scale that increment by the integer indices from 0 through length(t)−1, and add f1. This gives f1 at the first sample and f2 at the last sample.
